title: B-tree vs Hash Index
description: Compare B-tree and hash index structures for different query patterns

data.text: B-tree and hash indexes use fundamentally different data structures. B-tree supports range queries and sorting, while hash indexes offer fast equality lookups but limited range support.

data.title: B-tree characteristics
items: Supports equality, range, and prefix searches
Used by default in most databases

data.title: Hash characteristics
items: Collisions handled by chaining or open addressing

data.title: Hash index example
data.content: Create a hash index for exact-match session lookups.

data.title: Tip
data.text: Use B-tree by default. Choose hash only when you have pure equality predicates and the database supports memory-resident hash indexes well.

items.question: Does PostgreSQL support hash indexes well?
items.answer: Historically no. Hash indexes were not WAL-logged until PG10. B-tree is still safer for most cases.

items.question: Can I use both index types on the same column?
items.answer: Yes, but it is rarely beneficial. Choose the structure that matches your query pattern.

items.question: What about INMEMORY hash indexes?
items.answer: In-memory engines like MySQL HeatWave can use adaptive hash indexes automatically.

data.title: Summary
points: B-tree is the universal default for most queries
Hash excels at pure equality lookups
Hash cannot support ranges or sorting
Profile queries before choosing index types
data.takeaway: B-tree covers almost all production needs. Hash is a niche optimization for exact-match, high-throughput key lookups.
